source_text: Ἀνθρώπῳ δὲ ἀδύνατόν τι γνῶναι, καὶ παρὰ ἀνθρώπου μαθεῖν τὰ ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς, ἢ τὰ ἐπιόντα. Τίς γὰρ ἔσται ὁ μηνύσων; Ἄνθρωπος δὲ ὃς οὐκ οἶδεν εἰς τὴν ἀγαθὴν πορευθῆναι πόλιν, κάκωσιν ὑπομένει, τοῖς τε ὀφθαλμοῖς, καὶ τῷ παντὶ προσώπῳ. Πόλει δὲ ἐκείνῃ κακὰ προλέγω, ἧς ὅ τε βασιλεὺς νέος, καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες γαστρίμαργοι. Μακαρίζω δὲ γῆν τὴν ἀγαθὴν, ἧς βασιλεύει ὁ τοῦ ἐλευθέρου υἱός· ἔνθα εὐκαίρως ἀπολαύσουσιν ἀγαθῶν, οἱ ἐκεῖσε ἄρχειν ἠξιωμένοι. Ὀκνηρὸς δὲ καὶ ἀργὸς, οἶκον ἐλαττοῦσι χλευασταὶ γενόμενοι· καὶ εἰς τὴν ἑαυτῶν λαιμαργίαν, τοῖς πᾶσι καταχρώμενοι, ἀργυρίῳ ἀγώγιμοι, ἕνεκα ὀλίγου τιμήματος πάντα αἰσχρῶς καὶ ταπεινῶς πράσσειν ὑπομένοντες. Βασιλεῖ δὲ, καὶ ἄρχουσιν, ἢ δυνάσταις ὑπακούειν προσήκει, καὶ οὐκ ἀπεχθάνεσθαι, οὐδ᾽ ὅλως λυπηρόν τι εἰς αὐτοὺς ῥῆμα ἀποῤῥίπτειν. Δέος γὰρ, μὴ τὸ καὶ τὸ καταμόνας εἰρημένον, εἰς φανερόν πως ἔλθῃ. Τῷ γὰρ μόνῳ καὶ πλουσίῳ καὶ μεγάλῳ βασιλεῖ ἄγγελοι ὀξεῖς καὶ ὑπόπτεροι ἅπαντα διακομίζουσι, πνευματικὴν ὁμοῦ καὶ λογικὴν τελοῦντες ὑπηρεσίαν.
thought_title: Good and bad rulers; guard your words about the king
orientation: Good and bad rulers are set side by side, with a warning to guard even private words about the king.
pass_a_gloss: For a human it is impossible to know anything, and to learn from a human the things from the beginning or the things coming on. For who will be the one about to disclose? A man who does not know to go into the good city endures ill-treatment, both in the eyes and in the whole face. For that city I foretell evils, whose king is young, and the rulers gluttonous. I bless/call blessed the good land of which the son of the free man is king; where opportunely will enjoy good things those deemed worthy to rule there. The sluggish and idle (sg.) diminish a house, becoming mockers; and for their own gluttony, misusing all things, led by silver, for the sake of a little price enduring to do all things shamefully and basely. To a king and to rulers or dynasts it is fitting to obey, and not to be hated/make oneself hateful, nor at all to hurl any painful word at them. For there is fear lest the this-and-that spoken in private may somehow come into the open. For to the only and rich and great King swift and winged angels carry across all things, completing a service at once spiritual and rational.

pass_b_english: It is impossible for a human being to know, or to learn from another human being, anything of what was from the beginning or of what is still to come. For who will be there to tell him (Ecclesiastes 10:14)? The man who does not know how to make his way to the good city suffers harm in his eyes and in his whole face (Ecclesiastes 10:15). I foretell evils for that city whose king is young and whose rulers are gluttons (Ecclesiastes 10:16). But I call blessed the good land whose king is the son of a free man, where those found worthy to rule will enjoy good things at the proper time (Ecclesiastes 10:17).

The sluggish and the idle bring a house to decline, turning into mockers (Ecclesiastes 10:18). Squandering everything on their own gluttony, easily led by silver, they stoop to doing anything, shamefully and basely, for the sake of a small price (Ecclesiastes 10:19). It is right to obey a king, rulers, or men in power, and not to make oneself hateful to them, nor to fling any wounding word at them at all. For there is reason to fear that what is said even in private may somehow come into the open (Ecclesiastes 10:20). For to the only King, rich and great, swift and winged angels carry everything, performing a service at once spiritual and rational.
notes: Metaphrase of Ecclesiastes 10:14-20. 'The good city' follows Gregory; the LXX of Ecclesiastes 10:15 has only 'the city'. 'The son of a free man' renders the singular ὁ τοῦ ἐλευθέρου υἱός (the LXX has 'son of free men'). In 10:18 the subjects are singular (ὀκνηρὸς καὶ ἀργός) with a plural verb and participles; rendered as a plural class ('the sluggish and the idle'). τὸ καὶ τὸ καταμόνας εἰρημένον is the idiom 'this or that said in private', rendered 'what is said even in private'. The last sentence turns 'a bird of the air will carry the voice' (Ecclesiastes 10:20) into angels serving God; 'the only King, rich and great' is capitalized because it names God. Possible echoes of 1 Timothy 6:15 ('the only Sovereign, King of kings') and Hebrews 1:14 (ministering spirits) are left uncited as uncertain. No Psalm citations. The opening binds τι to 'what was from the beginning or is to come', as the 1622 Latin does ('vt homo ea, quae a principio fuerunt, aut postea futura sunt, cognoscat'); it is not a claim that a human being can know nothing at all. 'Bring a house to decline' renders οἶκον ἐλαττοῦσι (diminish; Latin 'domum minuunt').

changes: opening no longer says a human can know nothing at all: τι bound to 'what was from the beginning or is to come' (1622 Latin agrees)
'bring a house to ruin' -> 'bring a house to decline' (ἐλαττοῦσι = diminish)
'they will stoop' -> 'they stoop' (present participle ὑπομένοντες, no future)
'what is said even in private' kept: the 1622 Latin also reads καί as 'even' ('id etiam quod occulte')
